scenarios.title: Two Humanoids — Retail Backroom Fulfillment
scenarios.status: Closed — operations accepted; chain rollout held at financial gate
scenarios.summary: Deploy two humanoid robots in an unchanged, employee-only department-store backroom. A sales associate submits a stock-keeping unit, size, and color request from a tablet. A robot walks through existing human aisles and doors, uses the short stair route where required, retrieves a shoe box or already-hung garment, and delivers it to an employee handoff point. The same fleet performs put-away and cycle-count work between requests. Tangled hangers, ladders, electrical work, and customer-floor operation remain human tasks.
scenarios.decision: The 30-day pilot passed the safety, retrieval, wait-time, inventory-accuracy, damage, and intervention gates, so Meridian accepted the operating procedure and support handoff. Finance did not authorize chain rollout: measured annual gross value was $184,468 versus the $346,000 annual value required for five-year payback at the current planning cost. A second-site decision requires a binding vendor quote and either lower recurring cost or independently measured value at or above $346,000 per year.

scenarios.financial_note: There is no positive payback at the pilot inputs. The labor component is 4,965 hours × $26.64 per hour = $132,268, using the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics March 2026 retail-trade total-compensation benchmark. Adding $52,200 of fictional measured margin recovery produces $184,468 annual gross value, below the $218,000 recurring cost. Five-year payback requires $346,000 annual gross value: $218,000 recurring cost plus $128,000 annual recovery of the $640,000 installation. Robot, integration, license, and support prices are planning allowances pending binding quotes.

acceptance: Zero recordable safety events and all stop, route-block, network-loss, and human-yield tests passed
Retrieval mission success reached 98.1% against the 97% gate
Median associate wait fell from a fictional 7.1-minute baseline to 3.4 minutes
Inventory location accuracy reached 98.7% and damage or wrong-item rate was 0.2%

lessons: The human-form-factor rationale must be tied to actual doors, aisles, stairs, shelves, and handoff points
Tangled hangers and damaged packaging require an explicit human exception path
Operational acceptance and financial approval are separate decisions
Do not scale until vendor quotes and measured store value close the $161,532 annual value gap

scenarios.title: Three Quadrupeds — Night Security
scenarios.summary: Deploy three quadruped robots for human-supervised night patrol across stairs, curbs, gravel, and narrow walkways. Two robots run scheduled perimeter routes while the third rotates through charging and reserve coverage. Robots observe and report; authorized human security personnel retain all response decisions.
scenarios.decision: The pilot met all safety, privacy, patrol, alert, geofence, availability, and docking criteria. Sentinel Ridge authorized two recurring quadruped patrol posts and retained the existing fixed-post responder. Expansion beyond the approved routes requires a new route, privacy, network, and benefit review.
scenarios.financial_note: The arithmetic is reproducible, but this remains a planning model. The $100,000-per-robot public price anchor excludes the configured security system; all payload, dock, integration, support, customs, and site costs require quotes. With fictional customer inputs of two 10-hour contracted rover posts at $45 per hour plus $15,000 vehicle cost, simple payback is 3.22 years. Removing only one post produces an 11.73-year payback and fails the five-year screen.

scenarios.title: AD-01 Autonomous Tote Transfer Robot — First Sale
scenarios.summary: Develop a compact mobile manipulator that moves one approved tote type weighing up to 15 kilograms along an 18-meter indoor route between two fixed stations. The program runs from observed customer workflows through Engineering Verification Test, Design Verification Test, Production Validation Test, first-customer deployment, 30-day acceptance, and a commercial release decision.
scenarios.decision: Leadership approved limited availability for the narrow two-station workflow. The first customer accepted the system, Cost of Goods Sold and pilot-build yield met the release gate, and the corrected design exceeded the mission target. General Availability remains gated by actuator second-source qualification and a qualified pipeline that can support the 82-unit development break-even screen.

scenarios.financial_note: These are fictional concept-stage inputs, not quoted economics. Customer simple payback is 1.96 years at the documented workload and public labor benchmark. At the $285,000 unit price and $150,000 Cost of Goods Sold ceiling, contribution is $135,000 per unit and 82 units are required to recover the $10.975M development authorization before sales, warranty, support, overhead, working capital, tax, and financing.

scenarios.title: Robotics Support & Field Operations
scenarios.status: Closed — service owner accepted operating model
scenarios.summary: Stand up one traceable support chain for 250 humanoid and quadruped robots across 60 sites. The operating model connects Salesforce customer cases, ServiceNow or Zendesk workflows, field work, Jira engineering defects, robot telemetry, parts, knowledge, release readiness, and customer communications.
scenarios.decision: The executive sponsor and service owner accepted the 180-day operating model. All 250 robots and 60 sites have owned installed-product records; severity, on-call, field, parts, remote-access, continuity, and product-readiness controls are live. High-confidence predictive case automation remains a phase-two improvement and is not required for closeout.

scenarios.financial_note: The arithmetic is reconciled, but the 250-robot installed base, demand rates, staffing costs, and platform amounts are fictional planning inputs. scenarios.title: Two Humanoids — Airport Restroom Cleaning Pilot
scenarios.status: Closed — pilot accepted; expansion held at economics gate
scenarios.summary: Deploy two humanoid robots into four unchanged Terminal 4 public restrooms for controlled routine cleaning and replenishment. The rooms remain closed and verified empty during robot work. Airport custodians retain inspection, prohibited-contamination response, corrective cleaning, supply custody, and reopening authority. The program is managed through three coordinated viewpoints: seller/integrator, humanoid manufacturer, and airport buyer/operator.
scenarios.decision: The airport accepted the seller's pilot deliverables, the manufacturer froze a four-room pilot product baseline, and airport operations accepted the controlled runbook. Expansion was not authorized. The pilot passed safety, mission, quality, supply, support, and cost gates, but $68,985 of annualized routine-task capacity does not support the $3.1345 million five-year planning Total Cost of Ownership. A scale decision requires binding quotes and measured non-labor service value.

phases.name: Airport site, safety, privacy, and network

scenarios.financial_note: The equipment and service amounts are quote-required planning allowances, not vendor prices. Four rooms × three missions per day × 0.50 observed labor-hour × 365 days creates 2,190 annual task-hours. At the fictional airport loaded rate of $31.50 per hour, annual capacity value is $68,985. Capacity is not cash savings, no job is eliminated, and even the low-cost/high-value sensitivity fails five-year cost recovery.
